idiom_name: props-only function component fed by a custom hook (supply half) at the route or page component
implementation_notes: The presentational half is an ordinary function component that renders props and calls the callbacks it was given: no store import, no fetch, no context lookup beyond what it was handed. The supply half moved into a custom hook - React's documentation describes custom hooks as the way to share stateful logic between components - and once the fetching, subscription and error handling live in useCart(), the wrapping container component is unnecessary: the page component calls the hook and passes the result down as props. The classic container stays justified when the data source must be injectable per screen (tests, stories, route boundaries), when the same markup renders under different sources, or in a codebase whose containers were generated by connect() or a similar higher-order component.
pitfalls: A 'presentational' component that imports a store, a fetch helper or a context it was not handed is a container with a misleading name.
Copying a prop into local state freezes the child on its first value; keep the view controlled and drive it from props.
A hook that returns a fresh object (and fresh callbacks) on every render re-renders every child unless those values are memoised.

variants.name: Container generated by a connect-style higher-order component
variants.idiom_name: higher-order component (connect-style) injecting data and callbacks as props
variants.implementation_notes: The classic container is generated rather than written: a higher-order component such as react-redux's connect() subscribes to the store and injects data plus bound action creators as props, so the presentational component underneath never learns where they came from. This is the shape the original 2015 article describes - containers 'usually generated using higher order components ... rather than written by hand' - and it is still what large legacy codebases and some libraries ship. Prefer the hook variant in new code: it removes the wrapper, keeps the props typed by the caller and avoids stacking wrappers.
pitfalls: Wrapper stacking: several connect/HOC layers per screen make prop provenance hard to trace and complicated to type.
Shallow equality on mapped props causes re-renders the presentational child cannot prevent; memoise the selectors.
An injected prop that shadows a store read inside the component hides a second data path; the view must use only what it was given.
